newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria president appeals for NATO membership.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria president appeals for NATO membership.

text.p: Bulgaria's admission to NATO would boost political and economic links with the members of the alliance, President Petar Stoyanov said on Monday.

In a television address broadcast after the caretaker government adopted a declaration stating its desire for full NATO membership, Stoyanov said:"To us membership in NATO is as much a matter of policy and joint exercises, as industry, economy and trade."
"Today's decision of the government echoes the will of a huge majority of Bulgarians, who feel inseparable from the free world," said Stoyanov.

The declaration adopted in an effort to clarify Sofia's so far ambiguous position on the issue, also aims to qualify the Balkan country for membership nomination at a NATO summit in July, where the alliance will decide which new members to admit.

It coincides with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright starting an 11-day trip to nine world capitals to unveil NATO expansion plans and to persuade Russia to agree by the July summit on a charter defining a special relationship with the alliance.
"We should not allow Bulgaria to end up in a grey area of obscurity on the political map of Europe," said Stoyanov.
"Bulgaria will not wake up in NATO tomorrow. First we have to resolve the crisis...but we should not miss the steps which are strategically important for Bulgaria," he added.

Reform-laggard Bulgaria has fallen behind top contenders in the race for memebership such as Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, although like most ex-communist states, it takes part in NATO's Partnership for Peace initiative designed to foster cooperation between former Cold War foes.
"Accession will not be cheap, but we are bound to pay a much higher price if we remain outside NATO," said Stoyanov.
The caretaker cabinet, appointed by Stoyanov last week, inherited from the former Socialist administration crippling fuel and grain shortages, enormous debts and empty coffers.
"We would not like to let our economic crisis to hinder development of foreign policy," said earlier Foreign Minister Stoyan Stalev.
In the declaration, shortly to be presented to NATO headquarters, Bulgaria states its will to be invited to accession talks, Stalev said.

Despite a 1993 parliamentary declaration stating Bulgaria's desire to join the alliance, the ruling Socialists have fudged the issue over the past two years because of traditionally warm ties with Russia, which strongly opposes NATO's eastward expansion.

The Socialists stepped down from power two weeks ago and 20 months before the end of their term, bowing to opposition demands for early elections after 30 days of mass protests fuelled by economic hardship.

Stoyanov, elected on the opposition ticket in November, stated Bulgaria's clear intention to join the alliance immediately after taking office in January during a visit to NATO headquarters in Brussels.
The opposition Union of Democratic Forces, the favorite to win general elections on April 19, has traditionally supported Bulgaria's bid to join the North Atlalntic Treaty Organisation.
"With today's declaration all Bulgarian institutions, the President, the Parliament (in 1993) and the Government have said 'yes' to NATO," said Stoyanov.
